To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the pronunciation of pseudowords is influenced by the pronunciation of related words and by the visual appearance of those pseudowords.

the pronunciation of pseudowords is facilitated when the pseudoword is preceded by a semantically related word, and the pronunciation of pseudonyms is facilitated when the word is visually similar to a word that is semantically related to the pseudonym.
the pronunciation of a pseudoword is influenced by lexical activation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
lexical contributions to pseudowords, which are pronounceable novel strings with no lexical entry.
the role of lexical knowledge in pseudoword production.
the role of the lexicon in the pronunciation of novel strings.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
lexical contributions to pseudowords are possible, but that they are not obligatory.
lexical contributions to the pronunciation of pseudowords are not only possible, but likely, under some conditions.
lexical information does influence the pronunciation of pseudowords.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
lexical contributions to the pronunciation of pseudowords are not automatic, but are activated by the presence of a lexical item with the same spelling pattern.

lexical contributions to pseudowords may be limited to those cases where the pseudoword is highly similar to a word in the lexicon, but that the lexical contribution can be substantial in those cases.
lexical information is activated in the pronunciation of novel forms and that this information can be used to constrain the pronunciation of pseudowords.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the pronunciation of pseudowords can be influenced by lexical information.
the pronunciation of a nonword can be influenced by lexical activity, and the nature of this influence can be investigated by using the logic of spreading-activation models of lexical access.
